chunks: I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'Perhaps (sometimes) the shares (of inheritance) are increased until they become a hundred, or less, or more.' So he said: 'They do not exceed six.'

Then he said: 'Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) used to say: Indeed, the One Who counted the grains of sand of 'Alij certainly knows that the shares of inheritance do not exceed six. If they perceived its principle, they would not exceed six.'

key_terms.أُعِيلَ: 'Awl — the Sunni doctrine that when legislated shares sum to more than 1, each share is proportionally reduced; rejected in Shia fiqh
key_terms.السِّهَامُ: Legislated shares (sihham) — the fixed fractional portions of an estate (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/6, 1/3, 2/3) prescribed in Quran 4:11-12
key_terms.رَمْلَ عَالِجٍ: Sand of 'Alij — proverbial reference to countless grains, emphasizing God's absolute knowledge and precision

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia position on 'awl (increasing inheritance shares) according to Al-Kafi?
ai.summary: Abu Basir reports a jurisprudential ruling from Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) on the question of 'awl — the controversial Sunni doctrine that inheritance shares can exceed their designated fractions (e.g., summing to more than 1). The Imam firmly rejected this practice, citing Imam Ali's authoritative statement grounding the ruling in divine knowledge. Imam Ali's argument invokes God's omniscience: the same God Who counted the innumerable grains of desert sand determined that inheritance shares never exceed six base fractions, eliminating any need for 'awl. This hadith is a key Shia legal argument against the 'awl doctrine accepted by the majority Sunni schools.
